title: Abot kamay: Embedding digital transactions in the Philippines
tldr: An ethnographic study of three Metro Manila communities shows Filipino digital transaction adoption is driven by cultural norms of reciprocal obligation and kinship support rather than by consumer convenience.
problem_and_motivation: Industry literature on digital finance in the Global South has focused on quantifying adoption while neglecting how local users give meaning to transaction platforms within established cultural and social norms. The paper investigates how everyday dynamics of exchange in the Philippines are being remediated via digital transactions, using Polanyi's concept of embeddedness to ground analysis.
approach: Ethnographic multi-sited study conducted across three Metro Manila districts with differing socio-economic profiles from 2019 to 2022.
Three cohorts were studied: middle-aged employed householders in Santa Mesa, precarious informal workers in Payatas, and college-educated digital-economy freelancers in Quezon City.
Data collection involved semi-structured focus groups of eight to ten participants conducted in Tagalog at communal meeting spaces.
Individual video-link interviews replaced focus groups for the Quezon City cohort after COVID-19 separation of the research team in March 2020.
The analysis applies Polanyi's framework of reciprocity, redistribution, and remuneration alongside Braudel's multi-layered economy concept.
findings: num: 72% mobile digital penetration with 44% of adults remaining unbanked in the Philippines.
num: Digital transactions reached 42.1% of retail payments by 2022 with P2P transfers growing at 91.2% per annum.
num: GCash had 76 million users by 2023, emerging as the clear market leader.
All three cohorts articulated adoption of digital transactions in terms of social relationships and reciprocal obligations rather than convenience.
Santa Mesa participants preferred cash on delivery and used digital platforms mainly for online shopping and managing social obligations.
Payatas participants used GCash principally for money transfers to provincial relatives and receiving funds, reflecting redistribution priorities.
Quezon City freelancers employed GCash as a security intermediary between bank accounts and other transaction platforms.
Digital transactions were remediating existing informal lending practices such as the 5/6 money lending system with lower-cost alternatives like Home Credit.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This paper contributes a culturally grounded qualitative account of digital transaction adoption in the Philippines, demonstrating that everyday fintech usage is driven by social obligations and reciprocal norms rather than convenience alone. It extends Polanyi's framework of embeddedness to show how digital platforms simultaneously transform and are shaped by pre-existing cultural logics of reciprocity, redistribution, and remuneration. The three-cohort ethnographic design reveals how socio-economic position mediates the relationship between digital affordances and cultural practice, offering evidence that transaction platforms are becoming embedded as financial infrastructure for social reproduction in the Global South.
directly_justifies: Filipino digital transaction adoption is driven by reciprocal social obligations rather than by convenience.
Digital platforms are remediating existing practices of abot kamay across time and space for all cohorts studied.
num: P2P transfers via transaction platforms grew at 91.2% per annum by mid-2023.
Young Payatas participants created novel transaction chains involving content monetization and gaming wagers via GCash.
GCash serves as a security intermediary between conventional bank accounts and third-party platforms for some users.
limits: The study is confined to three Metro Manila districts and cannot be generalized to rural or provincial populations.
Sample sizes for each cohort are modest, with eight to ten participants per focus group.
The COVID-19 pandemic disrupted the original multi-site research design, forcing a methodological shift for one cohort. [unacknowledged]
No systematic quantitative measurement of transaction volumes or behavioral frequency was conducted.
